title.narrative: Humanitarian and resilience building activities in Sri Lanka

description.narrative: This investment focused on Humanitarian and resilience building activities in Sri Lanka responding to COVID -19 and the 2022 economic crisis. It covered four agreements through disparate humanitarian response mechanisms including the United Nations Joint SDG Fund in Sri Lanka; the Australian Humanitarian Partnership (AHP) and Australia’s International Red Cross Partnership. This also included an agreement with the United Nations World Food Program in response to the 2022 Sri Lanka Humanitarian Needs Plan.

participating-org.narrative: AUSTRALIA - Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

organisation.narrative: Australia - Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

description.narrative: AKASA, an organisation dedicated to supporting women with disabilities, operates in Sri Lanka’s North Central region—an area marked by deep poverty and daily challenges, especially for women with disabilities. In this context, AKASA provides comprehensive support services to survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) living with disabilities. With funding from the Australian Government’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT), UNFPA implemented targeted capacity-building initiatives to strengthen AKASA’s ability to deliver high-quality, inclusive, and survivor-centred services. ‍ These interventions enhanced the quality and reach of AKASA’s support, ensuring that women with disabilities receive the care, protection, and empowerment they need on their journey toward recovery and dignity. Through this partnership, Australia continues to champion inclusive development and gender equality, helping build safer and more resilient communities.

Australia partnered with UNFPA to provide protection services to 296 survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) within shelters in seven districts. Survivors received information on GBV services, livelihood and skills training and psychosocial counselling for greater economic, social and physical security. ‍ Financial assistance was extended to shelters in critical areas to continue operations and provide emergency assistance, psycho-social support, counselling, and legal services. Fourteen pregnant and lactating mothers received access to maternal health care services.

Australia partnered with the WHO and the Ministry of Health to meet the needs of the public health system and strengthening the patient management capacity within COVID-19 treatment centres. To manage outbreaks, the initiative conducted a series of analytical activities and generated evidence-based reports. The results will contribute to the new health financing strategy and the overall health system recovery plan for Sri Lanka.

Australia supported WHO to strengthen the patient management capacity within COVID-19 treatment centres by equipping 50 Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure machines and 1415 SARS-COV-2 research panels. Australia partnered with UNOPS and Sri Lankan Ministry of Health to establish three oxygen concentrator plants for uninterrupted oxygen supply and 2 Genomic sequencing machines to identify variants of COVID-19. Australia partnered with UNDP to fund fully functional intermediate care centres with 600 beds, four five-function ICU beds, 1 high-end Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy (CRRT), and 1 Medical Waste Incinerator (Capacity 100 Kg/h). Through WHO, Australia procured 60 patient warmers for 9 public hospitals.

Australia supported the Departments of Agriculture, Health, and Education in implementing the Entrepreneurial School Garden (ESG) program and provided training to 104 Master Trainers/ Trainers of Trainers (ToT). In addition, 505 teachers from selected schools received training and technical advice on improving school gardens, eating habits, and the nutrition status of students through the ESG programme. In addition, with FAO, Australia provided training and equipment (drop irrigation system plastic mulch and insect proof nets) to 570 smallholder farmers. These helped strengthen food security among vulnerable groups at a time of severe economic distress.

Australia, through WHO, supported the strengthening of the Sri Lankan health system to adapt and respond to possible pandemics and other public health emergencies. Critical efforts included establishing 120 village-level committees to support local communities in improving health and well-being. In addition, WHO recommended comprehensive health financing policy and the identification of key policy reform options to safeguard Sri Lanka's primary healthcare approach, report evolving needs and improve health sector resilience. These recommendations will be consolidated into an evidence-backed policy options document to advance the Sustainable Development Goals.

During the Sri Lankan economic crisis, Australia's humanitarian funding provided immediate support to the most vulnerable, especially women and children. Australia partnered with the UN's Joint Humanitarian Needs and Priorities Plan providing relief packages to 512 vulnerable women-headed households. Australia partnered with UNFPA to provide 125,000 at-risk women and girls with information cards with gender-based violence helpline information. The program provided lifesaving support, case management, legal assistance, counselling services and psycho-social support through eleven shelters to help protect the survivors of SGBV, comprising 2283 direct and indirect beneficiaries.

Ensuring food security among children during the crisis, Australia supported World Vision's RISE Lanka project to implement a mid-day meal program across all 5 project locations, encompassing 107 preschools; 2,478 (girls 1,132, girls with disability 9, boys 1,331, boys with disability 6) children. Reports from the Medical Officers (MOH) based on weight measurements and school attendance records highlight significant weight gain and an increase in preschool attendance. The Public Health Inspectors (PHIs) were vital for conducting nutrition and hygiene awareness programs for preschool children, leading to improved health habits among children where 1957 (girls 979, boys 963, girls with disability 9, boys with disability 6) children received crucial awareness on nutrition and hygiene practices. Additionally, RISE Lanka started 50 home gardens at preschools collaborating with the preschool management societies. Parents and teachers as well as children work together in the gardens boosting both garden yield and the preschool meal program.

title.narrative: Climate adaptation, mitigation, environment and biodiversity

description.narrative: In 2022, Australia partnered with World Vision to extend humanitarian support through the RISE Lanka Project for a period of one year (Resilient, Inclusive and Sustainable Economic development for Sri Lanka). It was launched to support farmers in the agriculture and dairy sectors to uplift food affordability in 5 vulnerable locations- Rideemaliyadda, Welikanda, Bibile, Meegahakiula and Lunugala. Cash assistance and high-quality climate-resilient seeds were distributed to 11,301 farmers (4,504 female, 6,741 male, including 56 Persons with disabilities). This allowed them to resume farming activities. The project partnered with government stakeholders, including the Mahaweli Authority and Provincial Department of Animal Production and Health (DAPH) to support the sustainable development of livelihoods for 451 dairy farmers (140 Female, 304 Male and 7 Persons with disabilities). The project also empowered 3,236 paddy farmers to engage in self-seed production by promoting registered self-seeding grain, to support resilient and sustainable crops.

In 2022, Sri Lanka was hit with its worst economic crisis and hyperinflation since Independence. Through our Humanitarian support, Australia joined forces with the Departments of Agriculture, Health, and Education of Sri Lanka to implement the Entrepreneurial School Garden (ESG) program, a school-based initiative that integrated gardening and entrepreneurship education and provided training to 104 Master Trainers/ Trainers of Trainers (ToT). 505 teachers from selected schools received training and technical advice on improving school gardens, eating habits, and the nutrition status of students through this programme. In addition, with Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), Australia provided training and equipment including drip irrigation systems and insect proof nets to 570 smallholder farmers. These interventions supported vulnerable communities to strengthen their food security at a time of severe economic distress.

In 2024, with financial support from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT), 11 shelters for survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) across Sri Lanka were upgraded to improve service delivery and survivor care. Located in both urban and rural areas—including Colombo, Anuradhapura, Kandy (two shelters), Monaragala, Ratnapura, Jaffna, Mullaitivu, and Nuwara Eliya—these shelters were strategically selected to reach underserved communities. ‍ DFAT funding enabled the provision of essential furniture, electrical appliances, cooking utensils, training equipment, solar panels, and other infrastructure enhancements. The upgrades strengthened the shelters’ capacity to offer safe, continuous, and survivor-centred services. Survivors now have access to temporary accommodation, psychosocial counselling, legal referrals, vocational training, and reintegration support. A key outcome has been the increased ability of shelters to serve more survivors, particularly in rural areas where services were previously limited. The installation of solar panels in select shelters has provided sustainable and reliable energy access, especially in remote locations. This initiative has reinforced Sri Lanka’s GBV protection system, providing survivors with safe spaces to heal with dignity and support. It highlights the impact of targeted, collaborative investment in infrastructure that empowers and protects vulnerable populations.

Mother of five, Damayanthi Dissanayake, from Ratnapura, faced considerable challenges over the past four years. Her husband's work was decimated by COVID-19, the economic crisis and prolonged hospitalization. The premature birth of twins, one severely underweight, further strained finances. Damayanthi struggled to feed her children.
